newsitem.title: USA: U.S. probing China supercomputer diversions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. probing China supercomputer diversions.

text.p: The United States believes there may have been some diversion of U.S.-made supercomputers by China for military use and is reviewing the affected sales, U.S. officials said Tuesday.

"It is true that we are investigating some cases of super computer sales to China," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told the Senate Finance Committee. Her spokesman, Nicholas Burns, said later: "We are reviewing right now some of the supercomputer sales for possible diversion...We suspect there may have been some diversions in some cases."

Burns gave no details on the number or companies involved in the potential diversions. The New York Times reported in Tuesday's editions that the Commerce Department has been investigating last year's sale by Silicon Graphics of a supercomputer that performs almost six billion operations per second -- 10 times the speed of the fastest personal computer -- to a Chinese science academy.
It quoted the company as saying the buyer was a benign civilian institution but nuclear experts as saying the academy had other functions, like helping China develop long-range missiles.

The newspaper also reported that the Justice Department was investigating another Silicon Graphics computer sale in 1996 to a Russian research institute that also served as a nuclear weapons laboratory.

The Clinton administration deregulated the export of computers in 1995 on the grounds that supercomputers were becoming more powerful and increasingly available worldwide with the United States holding a comparative advantage in the technology. But it made special provision for licensing supercomputers to China to insure against sales for military end use, officials said.
